title: Every Exam Question Stayed Identical, Yet One Cover Line Tanked Scores
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Claude Steele & Joshua Aronson (1995): Stereotype Threat — How Working-Memory Anxiety Hijacks High-Stakes Tests, grounded in Claude M. Steele, Joshua Aronson (1995) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1995 at Stanford University, Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson gave high-achieving Black and White Stanford undergraduates an identical 30-minute set of the hardest verbal items from the Graduate Record Examination (GRE), statistically controlling for baseline SAT scores.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that only ONE sentence changed at the top of the room: in the 'Diagnostic' condition, students were told the test measured genuine 'personal intellectual ability and verbal limitations'; in the 'Non-Diagnostic' condition, the EXACT SAME booklet was introduced as a 'laboratory study of psychological problem-solving mechanics unrelated to ability'.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Claude M. Steele, Joshua Aronson (1995). Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.69.5.797
- Claude M. Steele, Joshua A. Aronson (2004). Stereotype Threat Does Not Live by Steele and Aronson (1995) Alone. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066x.59.1.47
- Henry Louis Gates, Claude M. Steele (2009). A CONVERSATION WITH CLAUDE M. STEELE. Du Bois Review: Social Science Research on Race. https://doi.org/10.1017/s1742058x09990233

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
